claims.claim: Product–market fit is used in entrepreneurship education as a customer-centered concept that rejects assuming customers will come merely because an offering is built.
Product–market fit is best treated here as a context-dependent degree of match between a specific offering and a defined market, not as a permanent certification or guaranteed outcome.
Actual customer behavior and opinion research are quantitative evidence, while qualitative evidence can help explain why and how customers respond; the two evidence types answer different questions.
For freemium applications, retention is important for understanding repeated customer relationships, but the research literature does not have one consensus definition of retention.
A retention figure is more interpretable when it identifies the cohort, starting event, return behavior, and observation period; definitions and measurement choices affect the result.
Attention measures such as views, signups, and downloads can indicate awareness or initial interest but do not alone establish sustained customer value or product–market fit.
Repeated behavior can still have alternative explanations, so favorable metrics support a limited inference rather than proving causation, future demand, profitability, or venture success.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Product–market fit has no single authoritative universal metric or threshold.
positions: Entrepreneurship teaching materials describe customer-centered, iterative learning toward fit.
Retention research finds multiple definitions of retention and measurement choices.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson does not prescribe a pass/fail threshold. It explains fit as a bounded inference and requires contextual definitions for behavioral signals.
